finding: A confirmed 2027 tax measure is absent. ZATCA announced on 19 Nov 2026 that the Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax (DMTT, OECD Pillar Two) takes effect on 1 Jan 2027. It covers constituent entities of multinational groups with consolidated revenue of at least EUR 750m and tops the effective tax rate up to 15%. Saudi banks with foreign branches or subsidiaries (e.g. SNB in Turkiye and Pakistan, Al Rajhi abroad) pay mainly Zakat, which may not count as a covered tax, so their GloBE effective tax rate could fall below 15%. Aramco-group entities (including Petro Rabigh, about 60% owned), ADES and Bahri may also be in scope. Neither items.csv, the assessment nor impacts.csv mentions it, although its start date is the same as the tariff rise.
evidence: saudigazette.com.sa/article/666380 (19 Nov 2026, citing ZATCA release); argaam.com/en/article/articledetail/id/1956367 (25 Nov 2026: Maaden expects to fall in scope)
recommendation: Add an item from the ZATCA primary release. Add a tax/Zakat channel row for Banks and Energy: direction Negative; significance not determinable until the executive regulations; confidence Low; depends_on_execution = regulations. List which companies are likely in scope (foreign operations plus the revenue threshold).

finding: Wrong evidence for the claim that higher rates hurt term-funded banks. SAIB's margin proxy (NSCI/average assets) rose in the hiking year, from 2.70% (FY2022) to 2.86% (FY2023). It compressed only in the cutting years, to 2.46% (FY2024), 2.14% (FY2025) and 1.99% (9M 2026). The cited fall from 2.7% to 2.1% between FY2022 and FY2025 therefore happened while SAMA was cutting rates and does not show harm from higher rates. Bank Aljazira fits the claim (2.38% to 1.94% in FY2023); SAIB does not.
recommendation: Remove the SAIB example, or restate it as sensitivity to rate cuts. Derive rate sensitivity from each bank's observed margin response in the FY2023 hikes and the FY2024-25 cuts, not from deposit mix alone. Lower P-B-04 confidence to Low.

finding: The assumed rate direction for the two demand-deposit-rich banks conflicts with the dataset. In the FY2023 hiking year the margin proxy fell at Al Rajhi (3.20% to 2.71%) and at SNB (2.83% to 2.72%). It rose at corporate-heavy banks: Riyad 2.93% to 3.33%, SAB 2.52% to 3.08%, ANB 2.78% to 3.35% and BSF 2.87% to 3.23%. Al Rajhi's margin then recovered as rates were cut (2.96% FY2025; 3.19% 9M 2026). This is consistent with a largely fixed-rate retail and Islamic financing book. The +25bp hike in Sep 2026 is therefore more likely negative than cushioned for Al Rajhi. The claim that SNB gets 'the most benefit from higher rates' is also unsupported, and SNB's 66% demand share includes deposits of its international operations.
evidence: dataset.json NSCI_YLD FY2022-9M2026 per bank; argaam 1955163 (19 Nov 2026) on consolidation scope of listed-bank deposits
recommendation: Add the asset-repricing structure (fixed-rate retail/Islamic financing versus floating corporate) to deposit mix. Reverse or neutralise the rate effect for Al Rajhi and SNB, or set it as 'not determinable'. Cite the dataset ratios.

finding: The 'SAR 235bn ≈ 7.6% of deposits' figure. The arithmetic is 235.443/3,075.74 = 7.65%, which rounds to 7.7%, not 7.6%. More important, it overstates the drain on bank deposits. (a) It is a gross 9-month flow set against a stock; domestic principal repaid was SAR 42.8bn, so net new domestic debt was SAR 192.6bn, or 6.3% of deposits. (b) The total includes an early repurchase of more than SAR 17bn that was settled in new sukuk, so no new cash was raised. (c) It includes 'government alternative funding'. (d) Public SAR sukuk auctions raised only about SAR 72bn Jan-Sep (plus the 17.2bn exchange). The rest came through private channels, partly bank loans to government, which are bank assets rather than lost deposits. (e) Non-banks (GOSI, PIF, funds) also buy.
evidence: MoF Q3 2026 report (domestic issuance 235,443mn; domestic principal repaid 42,831mn; domestic debt 943,354mn to 1,135,965mn); Budget Statement FY2027 pp.48-49; NDMC monthly notices (F-090); Argaam 1955163 (deposits 3,075.74bn)
recommendation: Restate as 'gross domestic borrowing equal to about 7.7% of bank deposits (net about 6.3%); the share absorbed by banks is not disclosed'. Do not present it as a measure of deposits drained.

finding: The direction 'Negative (funding costs), High' rests on the sentence about borrowing channels, not on a larger financing need. The final budget implies a smaller net borrowing need in 2027: debt rises by SAR 190bn (1,733 to 1,923), against SAR 214bn in 2026e (1,519 to 1,733) and SAR 255bn already reached by Q3 2026. The full 2026 need of SAR 297bn had been raised by Q3 (SAR 298bn). 'Private market channels' were mostly ECA and international syndicated loans in 2025-26 (USD 13bn syndicated, NEXI, Bpifrance), not domestic deposits. Fitch also names an offset the row omits: higher oil revenue, if spent, creates deposits.
evidence: Budget Statement FY2027 p.49 and p.51 table; MoF Q3 2026 report; NDMC ABP 2026 (F-083: 2025 private 52%); F-089; Fitch via Arab News 18 Nov 2026
recommendation: Lower significance to Medium and confidence to Low-Medium until the NDMC 2027 borrowing plan is out. Add the oil-revenue and deposit-creation offset to the rationale.

finding: The government-deposit channel is missing. Fitch says government-entity deposits at SAMA were about SAR 370bn at end-Sep 2026, near a five-year low, and that government-related deposits are about one-third of bank deposits. That leaves less government liquidity to move to banks. B-013 is not cited in P-B-01, and Section 1 states 'Government deposits at SAMA are held at SAR 399bn' without noting the different Fitch measure.
evidence: https://www.arabnews.com/finance/saudi-banks-face-tighter-liquidity-in-2027-as-funding-demand-rises-fitch-3012687 (18 Nov 2026); Budget Statement p.51 (reserves at SAMA 399)
recommendation: Add B-013 and the government-deposit channel to P-B-01. In Section 1, note that the 399bn is the budget's 'government reserves at SAMA' and that Fitch's narrower measure is about 370bn.

finding: The row uses the simple loan-to-deposit ratio of 107% (verified: listed banks 9M 2026 loans 3,311.0bn / deposits 3,093.6bn = 107.0%) as if it were the binding constraint. It omits that SAMA's regulatory LDR is below 85% at all ten listed banks, against a 90% cap. The listed-bank figures are also consolidated, including foreign operations.
evidence: dataset.json Banks sector totals 9M2026; B-012 (Argaam 1913086); Argaam 1955163
recommendation: Show both measures and explain that regulatory headroom exists, while the simple ratio signals reliance on wholesale funding.

finding: 'Borrowing will focus on domestic and private market channels' is presented as confirmed ('This is a confirmed financing strategy'). It is a stated intention in the final Budget Statement; the size, instruments and channel mix come only with the NDMC 2027 borrowing plan, which was not published as of NDMC's latest release (17 Nov 2026). The item is tagged MINISTERIAL_STATEMENT although it is text from the budget document.
recommendation: Label it 'stated financing intention in the final budget (plan pending)'. Move it from 'confirmed measures' or flag it as such, and retag F-085.

finding: The direction 'slower corporate loan growth' is not supported by its own evidence. (1) Fitch expects about 8% credit growth in 2027, above 2026 actual: system credit +7.3% y/y at Sep 2026 and listed-bank loans +6.4% 9M y/y. 'Slower' holds only against the 2022-25 trend (12.3% CAGR). (2) The MoF attributes the -2.1% capex change to accelerated military spending in 2026, not to civil project cuts. (3) 2027 capex of SAR 178bn is +10% on the FY2026 budget (162), general items including the mega-projects allocation rise 6%, and municipal services rise 12%.
evidence: https://www.mof.gov.sa/documents/d/group-328541/bud-2027-eng-final?download=true pp.56-57, p.105; F-093; dataset.json Banks LOANS growth 9M2026/9M2025 = 6.4%, CAGR 2022-25 = 12.3%; Fitch via Arab News 18 Nov 2026
recommendation: Restate as 'loan growth stays well below the 2022-25 trend; versus 2026 roughly flat to slightly higher (Fitch 8%)'. Set direction to Neutral/slightly Negative and confidence to Low. Keep project rescheduling as an unquantified signal.

finding: P-B-02 cites F-105 (press reports of giga-project scaling-back; secondary, search extracts only), although Section 2 states such reports 'are unverified and are not used in the assessment'.

finding: The PIF channel is absent. Giga-projects are sponsored by PIF and its companies, which are large domestic bank borrowers, so rescheduling reaches banks through PIF as well as the budget. The Minister explicitly linked government, PIF and NDF roles to avoiding crowding out in domestic financing markets. PIF also receives Aramco dividends and sold its 49% HUMAIN stake to Aramco (1 Nov 2026).
recommendation: Add a PIF and government-related-entity borrowing channel for Banks, plus the PIF-Aramco link for Energy. Mark it as a policy signal with Low confidence.

finding: Government equity sales and privatisation are not treated as a channel (only 'any government share sale' as an indicator). The Minister announced the move to a National Privatization Strategy with about 202 projects in the pipeline (about 200 contracts worth SAR 800bn since 2017). With deficits and debt rising, share sales, including Aramco, are a financing option. They affect Aramco's free float and supply overhang and banks' ECM and PPP lending.
evidence: https://www.spa.gov.sa/en/N2735399 (24 Nov 2026); E-052 note (last Aramco sale Jun 2024)
recommendation: Add as a policy signal: direction not determinable, confidence Low, with indicators.

finding: The conclusion that 'the net effect is uncertain in sign' assumes a symmetric reversal of the 9M 2026 price and volume effects. (+13.2pp and -9.8pp are percentage points of group revenue, per the 2222 narrative.) The analyst's own items point to an asymmetric 2027. Saudi required production is about 10.48 mb/d against 9M 2026 liquids of 8.9 mb/d, so volume rises by roughly 20-30%. EIA STEO has Brent at 85.78 in 2027 against 97.44 in 2026, a fall of about 12% (unverified extract). Aramco's CEO expects about 2 mb/d of extra demand for two years to rebuild inventories. MoF 'other revenues incl. oil' is nearly flat (787 vs 794). On these, the volume effect is likely to dominate unless security worsens.
evidence: narratives/2222.yaml price_volume_support; E-035; E-040; V-009 (arabnews Aramco Q3, 3 Nov 2026); Budget Statement p.51
recommendation: Quantify two or three scenarios (price and volume path) or state the assumption explicitly. Keep the direction conditional on Hormuz and Red Sea security. Label the pp as 'pp of group revenue'.

finding: 'Saudi crude ~9.2-10.6 mb/d in Oct 2026 vs 6.8 mb/d in Q2' mixes two series. 9.19 comes from OPEC secondary sources and 10.563 from Saudi direct communication, while the Q2 figure of 6.822 is secondary sources only (direct communication Q2 is about 6.67). The OPEC MOMR was not read (read_primary=N). The October figures are corroborated only by press reports.
evidence: WebSearch 26 Nov 2026: Al Jazeera 11 Nov 2026, CTV, oilprice.com (OPEC Nov MOMR: secondary sources 9.19; Saudi-reported 10.563)
recommendation: Use one series consistently (secondary sources 9.19 vs 6.82). Mark it as secondary/unverified primary.

finding: The direction 'Positive (small)' contradicts the row's own rationale. The budget changes only electricity and water tariffs and does not change Aramco's domestic fuel or feedstock prices. No confirmed 2027 measure raises Aramco's regulated prices, and the price-equalisation offset is acknowledged.
evidence: impacts.csv P-E-04 rationale; Budget Statement pp.55-56; E-048 (Saudi Gazette 1 Jan 2026)
recommendation: Set the direction to 'Neutral / not determinable until the January 2027 price notices'. Note whether the 61.6% subsidy cut to utilities changes the fuel prices charged to SEC (not stated).

finding: The marine insurance pool is applied to Bahri without evidence. The Minister says the pool was set up 'to help reduce insurance costs for shipments arriving at the Kingdom's ports', with the effect 'expected to become evident gradually as new insurance policies are issued'. That describes inbound cargo insurance. Nothing shows it covers hull or war-risk premiums on Bahri's export VLCCs.
recommendation: Remove it as a confirmed cost support for Bahri, or mark it as an unverified assumption. Reword the Energy opportunity 'Insurance-pool support for shipping'.

finding: Weak tariff channel; stronger cost channels are missing. The 23 halalas/kWh rate applies to 'industrial sector connected to the electricity transmission or distribution network'. The previous industrial rate is unverified (F-098 note), so the size of the increase is unknown. Petro Rabigh's power, steam and water are understood to come largely from a dedicated IWSPP (RAWEC); this needs checking in the AFS. Missing: Aramco feedstock and fuel price notices (E-049); the end of the Aramco/Sumitomo Zakat/tax reimbursement from 9 Oct 2025 (E-055), now that 9M 2026 net profit is SAR 6.7bn; and DMTT via the Aramco group (P-R-001).
evidence: saudigazette.com.sa/article/665754 (26 Oct 2026); argaam 1848575 (9 Oct 2025); argaam 1869885 (1 Jan 2026); dataset.json 2380 NI_ATTR 9M2026 6,702
recommendation: Verify Petro Rabigh's utility supply. Add the Zakat/tax and feedstock channels, cite E-049 and E-055, and keep the tariff effect 'not quantified'.

finding: The quantified 9M 2026 finance costs of SAR 976m vs 668m (+46%) reflect borrowings that rose to SAR 20.25bn after the Shelf Drilling acquisition. They do not reflect SAMA's +25bp hike or government domestic borrowing, so the cited evidence does not support the rate channel. The row also does not explain why ADES differs from Arabian Drilling: the CEO stresses global diversification through Shelf (Saudi segment -12.8% in FY2025), which dilutes Saudi budget exposure, while the Saipem deal (5 Saudi jack-ups, SAR 3.8bn backlog) adds some back.
recommendation: Attribute the finance-cost rise to acquisition debt. Add the geographic mix as the reason ADES's exposure differs from Arabian Drilling's. Lower the rate-channel weight.

finding: The quantification cites 'offshore rigs suspended from end-Mar 2026' but omits that on 12 Aug 2026 Arabian Drilling received notices to resume all remaining suspended offshore rigs, with 100% offshore utilisation expected by end-Q3 (E-056). High significance rests mainly on the company-specific refinancing of the SAR 2bn sukuk (3 Feb 2027; covenant waiver to 31 Mar 2027). The link to government borrowing crowding out the refinancing is asserted, not evidenced.
recommendation: Update the activity facts. Keep refinancing as a company risk and set confidence for the budget link to Low.

finding: Confidence High is too high and the mechanism is misstated. Under Basel III the countercyclical buffer is a CET1 buffer, so AT1 sukuk raise Tier 1 ratios but do not satisfy it (check against SAMA's CCyB rules). The SAR 34.5bn includes Al Rajhi's USD 600m Tier 2, and the source does not tie the issuance to the CCyB; Argaam's analysts list retained earnings and lower payouts as the main tools. The buffer has applied since 25 May 2026, so its incremental 2027 effect is small.
recommendation: Reword: the measure is confirmed (High) and the ROE effect is via retained capital and AT1 coupons as funding/T1 management (Medium). Drop 'meeting it with Tier 1 sukuk' unless SAMA's rules allow it.

finding: All ten bank rows have identical direction (Mixed), significance (Medium), confidence (Medium), evidence ids, dependencies and indicators. The text ranks exposure (e.g. SAIB 'most exposed', SAB 'more room to lend'), but the ratings do not differ. The company figures carry no evidence ids, only 'our data' or 'segment notes'. I recomputed the segment shares from evidence/*.yaml (FY2025 segment TOI / TOI: SNB retail 43.8% / wholesale 44.5%; Al Rajhi 49.3/25.2; Riyad 26.9/54.7; SAB 30.0/54.0; Alinma 46.6/27.1; BSF 28.7/51.9; ANB 38.3/43.1; Albilad 38.9/30.9; SAIB 27.1/48.5; Aljazira 52.2/30.1) and they match, as do the FY2025 LDRs and cost-to-income ratios.
evidence: evidence/<ticker>.yaml segment entries FY2025; dataset.json ratios LDR, CI
recommendation: Differentiate the significance and direction where the text ranks banks. Cite fact ids (e.g. 1180-FY2025-TOI and the segment evidence lines).

finding: The forward-looking rows use FY2025 loan-to-deposit ratios although 9M 2026 is available and has moved materially: Riyad 112.5% to 117.0%, SAB 92.4% to 99.9%, BSF 110.1% to 113.4%, SAIB 102.2% to 98.6%. SAB is still the lowest among the five largest banks, but the gap has narrowed.
evidence: dataset.json Banks ratios LDR FY2025 vs 9M2026
recommendation: Use 9M 2026 (latest), or show both.

finding: The rationale ('housing measures ... coincided with slower new mortgage lending') rests on the 2025 fall of 12%. The 2026 data show stabilisation: April ended nine monthly declines and August was SAR 5.87bn, flat y/y (V-014). The SAR 500 allowance and the Nitaqat wage floors raise salaries, which supports capacity for salary-based retail financing; this positive is not stated.
recommendation: Use 2026 data and add the income-support effect on retail credit capacity.

finding: The 61.6% cut in subsidies to electricity and water companies and the tariff rise change the cash flows and borrowing needs of SEC and NWC. Utilities are a fast-growing bank exposure (utilities credit +25.6%; USD 13bn syndicated loan for power and water), but this bank channel is not covered.
recommendation: Add a utilities-lending sub-channel or note it under P-B-02.

finding: The escalation after 30 Sep 2026 is not reflected in the base case. Bank Q3 filings (BSF, SAIB, SNB, Alinma) report a significant escalation after 30 Sep. The coalition reported 4 drones intercepted over Ras Tanura on 25 Nov, tankers were hit in Hormuz on 21 and 25 Nov, and Hormuz traffic was about 65% below pre-war in mid-Nov. The assessment's 'volume recovery and fading premium' story and Fitch's base case (Hormuz reopens in 1Q27) are not stress-tested. The credit-quality channel (ECL overlays, conflict-hit borrowers, development-fund repayment deferrals) has no row.
evidence: saudigazette.com.sa/article/666520 (25 Nov 2026); narratives/1050.yaml, 1030.yaml, 1180.yaml, 1150.yaml (subsequent events); E-021; F-056
recommendation: Add a security and credit-quality channel row and a downside scenario, and make the Energy volume direction explicitly conditional.

finding: 'Base dividend (+3.5% a year per company policy)': Aramco describes a 'sustainable and progressive' base dividend, and 3.5% is the realised increase, not a stated policy. 'Dividends paid SAR 320.4bn vs FCF SAR 320.4bn (our calculation)': both figures are Aramco-reported (FCF SAR 320.4bn/USD 85.4bn; total distributions SAR 320.4bn/USD 85.5bn). The dataset's FCF of 320,354 matches.
recommendation: Reword to 'recent increases of 3.5% a year' and 'distributions equal to FCF (company-reported)'.

finding: The 'quantified' fields hold historical 9M 2026 company results (realised price, Bahri revenue, Petro Rabigh profit) rather than quantified policy effects, and none of the cited evidence ids points to them. recommendation: Label them 'historical context (dataset fact ids ...)' and keep 'quantified' for policy effects or 'not quantified'.

finding: 'The Energy Minister plans to raise East-West Pipeline throughput to about 10 mb/d'. SPA says 'development plans are under consideration ... to around 10 million barrels per day in the coming years', and Aramco's CEO says preliminary engineering is under way with no FID.

finding: 'Debt rises to SAR 1,733bn at end-2026' is stated without noting that actual debt at end-Q3 2026 was already SAR 1,773.6bn, above the year-end estimate. The budget footnote says the actual may differ and that NDMC will publish it with the 2027 plan.

finding: The Nitaqat full-credit minimum wage rises to SAR 5,000 six months after the measures start, then to SAR 6,000 twelve months later. This labour-cost channel for companies employing Saudis (drillers, Bahri, banks) is not discussed.

finding: There is no explicit statement on Zakat or corporate tax changes for 2027. The budget shows 'other taxes (incl. Zakat)' at SAR 35bn vs 39bn in 2026e, and Zakat is a material cost for banks (e.g. Riyad's Zakat +20.3% in 9M 2026).

'Health spending (-16%)' partly reflects the transfer of health clusters to the Health Holding Company (a reclassification) and 2026 crisis spending.

finding: The quantified text says the law 'requires private-sector dues to be paid within set timeframes before new commitments'. The MoF release says it prohibits a government entity from awarding new contracts 'if it has failed to take the necessary action to address outstanding payments, as specified in the Implementing Regulations'. Timeframes and the effective date are not sourced, and the Cabinet approval (F-099) was merged into F-066 without its own URL.

finding: 'A smaller ... budget': spending falls 3% only against the 2026 estimated outturn. Against the FY2026 budget, 2027 spending is +6% (1,392 vs 1,313) and capex is +10% (178 vs 162).
